pulls.body:
Bumps the pip group with 2 updates in the /testing/plugins_integration directory: [pytest-mock](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest-mock) and [twisted](https://github.com/twisted/twisted). Updates `pytest-mock` from 3.16.0 to 3.17.0
Release notes

Sourced from pytest-mock's releases.

v3.17.0

2026-10-17

  • #641: Failures of mock assertions such as assert_called_with are again reported only once, instead of two or three times with the original error from the mock module chained before them.
  • #642: Mock assertion failures no longer show misleading introspection when they are not about the arguments of the last call: assert_called, assert_called_once, assert_not_called, assert_any_call, their await counterparts, and assert_called_once_with/assert_awaited_once_with when the mock was not called (awaited) exactly once. The introspection also no longer reports arguments passed by position versus by keyword as different for autospecced mocks, and no longer shows empty Args:/Kwargs: sections when assertion rewriting is not available.
  • #643: assert_has_calls and assert_has_awaits failures no longer show pytest introspection, which compared the expected and actual calls position by position and so reported differences between unrelated calls. The mock's own message, listing the expected and actual calls, is still shown.

v3.16.1

2026-10-17

  • #617: Fixed assert_has_calls raising ValueError instead of AssertionError (or showing misleading introspection) when the expected calls are plain tuples rather than call(...) objects, such as (args, kwargs) entries of another mock's call_args_list, (args,), (kwargs,), (name, args) or (name, kwargs).
  • #621: Fixed mocker.stop() sometimes stopping the wrong mock, for example with mocks from mocker.create_autospec.
  • #621: mocker.stop() now undoes the most recent patch first when the same object is used in several patches.
  • #623: Fixed misleading introspection in assert_has_awaits failures, and assert_has_calls/assert_has_awaits raising IndexError instead of AssertionError when calls is passed by keyword.
  • #624: Clear spy_return_iter after a spied synchronous or asynchronous function raises, matching spy_return.
  • #627: Document async_stub await assertions and the distinction between call and await tracking.
  • #629: Fixed mocker.resetall() skipping the mocks patched with mocker.patch.multiple(), both the ones it creates and the ones passed explicitly.
  • #630: mocker.resetall() now also resets spy_return and spy_exception of spies, like it already did for spy_return_list and spy_return_iter, and no longer overwrites attributes with these names on mocks that are not spies.
  • #633: Fixed spies on classmethod, staticmethod, builtins and classes returning a MagicMock instead of calling the spied code after mocker.resetall(side_effect=True). Resetting a spy's side_effect now goes back to calling the spied code, also clearing any side_effect set on the spy.

pulls.title: tests(plugin_integration): Bump pytest-asyncio to v1.4.1.post1.
pulls.body:
pytest-asyncio v1.4.0 specifies an upper bound of pytest<10 in it's package metadata. Pytest already uses v10 versions for developement, so pytest-asyncio fails to install in the plugin tests. This causes all CI builds to fails.

Pytest-asyncio v1.4.1.post1 removes the upper bound and this PR bumps the pytest-asyncio version. This fixes the plugin integration tests and unblocks merges.

see also https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/pull/15311#issuecomment-6555131442 and #15309

pulls.title: tmpdir: hand out numbered dirs from a per-prefix counter
pulls.body:
<!-- claude-projects-attribution: {"github_login":"RonnyPfannschmidt"} -->
_Requested by **Ronny** · [project thread](https://claude.ai/code/project/chan_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvR?thread=cmsg_016UJjZXYjfpXuyNsZWbXxvRStBm5SmoryYY9KZJ4WBT64)_

🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Closes #15254.

`TempPathFactory.mktemp()` and `tmp_path` used `make_numbered_dir()`, which lists the whole basetemp on every call to find the next free number. basetemp gains entries with every test (two directories and a `*current` symlink per test in the issue's reproducer), so a session does O(N²) work. At N=3000, profiling put 41 of 54 s in `find_prefixed`.

This PR is a simpler alternative to the stat-validated listing cache proposed in the issue. The factory keeps a per-prefix counter (`_next_number`, keyed by the lower-cased prefix):

- `mktemp(numbered=True)`, and through it `tmp_path` and pytester, counts from 0 without listing basetemp. The factory always creates basetemp itself (a fresh `pytest-N`, or a `--basetemp` it has just wiped).
- `mkdir` decides uniqueness. A name it fails on (a directory, file or dangling symlink already there, or a `PermissionError` on Windows for a name still being deleted) is skipped. After 10 failures in a row, basetemp is listed once to jump past the run. After 20, an `OSError` chained to the last error is raised, so a filesystem that reports every name as taken cannot make it loop forever.
- `make_numbered_dir()` and its other callers (the `pytest-of-<user>` session root) are unchanged.

## Behaviour differences

- `mktemp` numbers are no longer "greater than any existing one". Existing names are skipped instead, and the docstring now says so. With a basetemp the factory owns, that only matters for directories something else creates there.
- Numbers never go down. With main, a number freed by the `tmp_path` retention removal could be reused.
- On a case-sensitive filesystem, a foreign `X2` no longer pushes `x` past 2, because `mkdir` decides the collision. Main matched the listing case-insensitively.

Covered by tests: no listing in `mktemp`, unexpected entries (directory, file, dangling symlink), a run of 50 taken names (one listing), overlapping prefixes (`test_a` and `test_a1` both produce `test_a10`), the probing limit, and retries on other `OSError`s.

## Numbers

Reproducer from the issue (`pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider`, noisy cloud box, wall-clock):

| tests | main | this PR |
|---|---|---|
| 1000 | 3.9 s | ~3–4 s |
| 2000 | 10.9 s | ~3.5 s |
| 4000 | 37.3 s | ~7.5 s |

Run time now grows linearly. What remains is mkdir/symlink syscalls.

pulls.title: Add `agentverify` to the plugin list
pulls.body:
[agentverify](https://github.com/simukappu/agentverify) is a pytest plugin for regression-testing AI agents. It registers through the `pytest11` entry point and provides a `cassette` fixture, a `--cassette-mode` option, and an `agentverify` marker. The fixture records an agent's LLM calls and tool calls to a YAML cassette once, then replays them on later runs, and the assertions check the tool calls, step-to-step data flow, and token and latency budgets. It works with LangChain, Strands Agents, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Pydantic AI, Google ADK, and CrewAI.

The name does not start with `pytest-`, so this adds it to `ADDITIONAL_PROJECTS`, as was done for `logot` (#11972) and `databricks-labs-pytester` (#12826). The PyPI metadata has `Framework :: Pytest` and requires `pytest>=7`.

```python
import pytest
from agentverify import ToolCall, assert_tool_calls

@pytest.mark.agentverify
def test_weather_agent(cassette):
    with cassette("weather_agent.yaml", provider="openai") as rec:
        run_my_agent("What's the weather in Tokyo?")
    assert_tool_calls(rec.to_execution_result(), expected=[ToolCall("get_weather", {"city": "Tokyo"})])
```

Change: one line in `scripts/update-plugin-list.py`. No changelog entry, since it does not change pytest itself.

pulls.title: feat(mark): expose `pytest.ParameterSet` in public API (#13431)
pulls.body:
### Description

This PR addresses #13431 (part of the public API typing roadmap #7469) by exposing `ParameterSet` in the public `pytest` namespace as the return type of `pytest.param()`.

Currently, developers using `pytest.param` in typed helper functions that return parameter sets receive private import warnings (such as Pyright's `reportPrivateImportUsage`) when importing `ParameterSet` from `_pytest.mark.structures`.

### Summary of Changes

- **Public export**: Exposed `pytest.ParameterSet` in `src/pytest/__init__.py` and included it in `__all__`.
- **Module declaration**: Set `__module__ = "pytest"` on `ParameterSet`.
- **Private constructor**: Refactored `ParameterSet` as a `NamedTuple` subclass with a `__new__` constructor that calls `check_ispytest(_ispytest)` so direct instantiation issues a `PytestDeprecationWarning`, while internal factories (`pytest.param()`, `extract_from()`, etc.) instantiate with `_ispytest=True`.
- **Factory methods**: Marked internal classmethods (`param`, `extract_from`) with `:meta private:` so Sphinx autodoc does not surface them under `pytest.ParameterSet`.
- **Documentation**: Added `pytest.ParameterSet` to `doc/en/reference/reference.rst` under `Objects`, and removed the obsolete entry from `nitpick_ignore` in `doc/en/conf.py`.
- **Changelog**: Added `changelog/13431.improvement.rst`.
- **Tests**: Added comprehensive unit tests in `testing/test_mark.py` verifying public export, `isinstance` checking, deprecation warning on unflagged initialization, and `pickle` serialization.
- **Authors**: Added myself to `AUTHORS`.

Closes #13431.

issues.title: rm_rf: empty directory under a read-only parent aborts removal; whole session basetemp left as garbage-*
issues.body:
`rm_rf` raises when it has to remove an **empty directory whose parent has lost owner write**. The exception escapes `shutil.rmtree`, and `maybe_delete_a_numbered_dir` swallows it as an `OSError`. So a single test that leaves this shape behind keeps that session's **entire** basetemp on disk as `garbage-<uuid>`. Every later session retries the same tree and fails the same way, so garbage builds up until the temp filesystem fills. On a CI host with a RAM-backed `/tmp` and a large suite, that's several GB per session.

Reproduced on pytest 9.0.3 and 9.2.0 (Linux, CPython 3.13).

### Minimal reproduction

```python
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path
from _pytest.pathlib import rm_rf

root = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / "tree"
leaf = root / "a" / "b"
leaf.mkdir(parents=True)
(root / "a").chmod(0o500)   # parent of an EMPTY directory loses write
leaf.chmod(0o500)

rm_rf(root)   # PermissionError: [Errno 13] Permission denied: '.../tree/a/b'
```

The same thing through the normal fixture lifecycle:

```python
# test_leak.py
def test_leaves_empty_readonly_chain(tmp_path):
    leaf = tmp_path / "a" / "b"
    leaf.mkdir(parents=True)
    (tmp_path / "a").chmod(0o500)
    leaf.chmod(0o500)
```

```
$ export PYTEST_DEBUG_TEMPROOT=$(mktemp -d)
$ for i in 1 2 3 4 5; do pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider test_leak.py; done
$ ls $PYTEST_DEBUG_TEMPROOT/pytest-of-$USER
garbage-09de7380-...  garbage-f4431b1e-...  pytest-2  pytest-3  pytest-4  pytest-current
```

### Cause

In `on_rm_rf_error`, the "chmod + retry" path walks upward and restores the parents **only when the failing path is a file**:

```python
    if p.is_file():
        for parent in p.parents:
            _chmod_rwx(str(parent))
            if parent == start_path:
                break
    _chmod_rwx(str(path))

    func(path)
    return True
```

When `func` is `os.rmdir` on an empty directory, the failure comes from the **parent** lacking write. The handler chmods only the directory itself, then retries `func(path)`. The retry raises the same `PermissionError` out of the error handler, which aborts the whole `rmtree`. `maybe_delete_a_numbered_dir` has already renamed the directory to `garbage-<uuid>` and then catches the `OSError`, so nothing reports it and the tree stays.

The traversal branch added for missing `S_IXUSR` (`func in (os.open, os.scandir)`, see #7940) already fixes the parent, bounded by `start_path`. The `os.rmdir` case needs the same treatment: for a failing directory, restore the parent (never above `start_path`) before retrying. Making the retry itself non-fatal, so that one bad entry can't abandon the rest of the tree, would also stop a single test from keeping a whole session's basetemp alive.

Related: #7821 (the `chmod(0)` variant of limited-permission directories not being removed).

issues.title: pytest 9.2.0 regression on Python 3.10.0: NodeId.__str__ raises AttributeError
issues.body:
### Description

pytest 9.2.0 introduced the internal `NodeId` dataclass as part of #14758.

The class uses `@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True, slots=True, kw_only=True)` and declares `_str_cache` with `default=None` and `init=False`.

CPython 3.10.0 has a known bug where slotted dataclass fields with `init=False` and a default value are not initialized. This was fixed in CPython 3.10.1 (python/cpython#88815).

Because `NodeId.__str__()` accesses `self._str_cache` directly, an instance constructed on Python 3.10.0 can raise `AttributeError` during string conversion.

pytest 9.2.0 declares `requires-python = ">=3.10"`, which includes Python 3.10.0.

### Minimal reproduction

Using Python 3.10.0:

```bash
python -m pip install pytest==9.2.0
```

Then execute:

```python
from _pytest.nodeid import NodeId

node = NodeId(path="test_example.py")
print(str(node))
```

### Expected behavior

```text
test_example.py
```

### Predicted actual behavior on Python 3.10.0

```text
AttributeError: 'NodeId' object has no attribute '_str_cache'
```

**Verification status:** The failure is inferred from the pytest 9.2.0 source and the CPython 3.10.0 implementation. The exact reproducer still needs to be executed on Python 3.10.0.

### Root cause

In `src/_pytest/nodeid.py`:

```python
_str_cache: str | None = dataclasses.field(
    default=None, init=False,
    repr=False, compare=False
)
```

In Python 3.10.0, `dataclasses._field_init()` does not initialize this field when `init=False`, even though the generated class uses slots.

CPython 3.10.1 added the missing condition:

```python
if slots and f.default is not MISSING:
    globals[default_name] = f.default
    value = default_name
```

The new `NodeId` class relies on the corrected behavior.

### Suggested resolution

Would the maintainers consider one of the following?

1. Initialize `_str_cache` explicitly, for example using `__post_init__()` and `object.__setattr__()`, to preserve compatibility with Python 3.10.0.
2. If supporting Python 3.10.0 is not intended, clarify the minimum supported patch version and update the package metadata accordingly.
3. Consider adding a small compatibility smoke test for the earliest supported CPython patch release so similar regressions can be caught in CI.

### References

- pytest 9.2.0 implementation: https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/blob/9.2.0/src/_pytest/nodeid.py
- pytest change: #14758
- CPython bug: https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/88815
- CPython 3.10.0 implementation: https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.10.0/Lib/dataclasses.py
- CPython 3.10.1 fix: https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/v3.10.1/Lib/dataclasses.py

Thank you for considering this compatibility issue.

```python
    assert Decimal("NaN") == approx(Decimal("1.1"))
```

```
>       result: bool = abs(self.expected - actual) <= self.tolerance
E       decimal.InvalidOperation: [<class 'decimal.InvalidOperation'>]
src/_pytest/approx.py:602: InvalidOperation
```

The same happens for `approx(1)`, and inside a list or dict (`[Decimal("NaN")] == approx([Decimal("1.1")])`), with or without `nan_ok=True`. A float NaN in the same place just compares unequal.

`ApproxScalar.__eq__` checks for a NaN *expected* value (fixed for Decimal in #15006), but not for a NaN *actual* value. For floats that does not matter, because `nan <= tol` is simply `False`, but an ordering comparison with a Decimal NaN raises `InvalidOperation` under the default context.

Seen on main (08017d9), Python 3.12.0, Windows 11.

```
colorama  0.4.6
iniconfig 2.3.1
packaging 26.3
pluggy    1.7.0
Pygments  2.21.0
pytest    10.0.0.dev21+g08017d9ad
```

A possible fix is to return `False` before the tolerance check when `actual` is a Decimal NaN. I have that change with tests locally (the approx suite passes) and can open a PR if this approach is fine.

This issue was prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code); I checked the reproduction and the code path myself.

issues.title: --doctest-modules uses GBs of memory on modules importing unittest.mock.call when the recursion limit is raised
issues.body:
🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Found while working on #15281 / #15283. This is a separate problem that already exists in 9.1.1, not the 9.2.0 regression.

## Reproducer

`conftest.py`:

```python
import sys

sys.setrecursionlimit(30_000)
```

`mod_c.py`:

```python
"""
>>> 1
1
"""
from unittest.mock import call
```

```
pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider --doctest-modules
```

Measured on Python 3.13, Linux:

| pytest | wall | peak RSS |
|---|---|---|
| 9.1.1 | 4.7 s | 5.2 GB |
| main (with #15283) | 6.2 s | 5.2 GB |

At a limit of 100 000 the process is OOM-killed.

## Cause

On Python 3.10+, the stdlib `DocTestFinder._is_routine` calls `inspect.unwrap(obj)` on every module attribute and only catches `ValueError`. `mock.call.__wrapped__` keeps returning a new `_Call` with a longer name, so unwrapping runs until `sys.getrecursionlimit()`. Memory grows roughly quadratically with the limit.

pytest used to guard against this. `MockAwareDocTestFinder._find` skipped `_is_mocked` objects and ran the stdlib `_find` under `_patch_unwrap_mock_aware()` (#3456, python/cpython#69718). That override was limited to Python < 3.10 and was removed along with 3.9 support in bb712f151. `_patch_unwrap_mock_aware` itself is now only used by its own test.

## Possible fix

Restore the `_find` override for all Python versions (about 14 lines in `src/_pytest/doctest.py`). I prototyped it locally: the reproducer drops to 0.09 s / 33 MB and the full test suite passes. A regression test is still needed.

issues.title: BaseExceptionGroup during fixture teardown skips remaining finalizers and reuses a cached function-scoped fixture
issues.body:
## Summary

A yield fixture raising a `BaseExceptionGroup` containing `asyncio.CancelledError`
or `GeneratorExit` during teardown prevents remaining finalizers of the current
item from running. A dependent function-scoped owner is not released and its cached
value can be reused by the next test. Ordinary `RuntimeError` does not have this
effect.

This is reproducible using pytest alone, with plugin autoload disabled. There is
no asyncio plugin, application code, monkeypatch of pytest, or custom test runner.

## Environment

- Python 3.13.3, Windows
- pytest 8.4.1
- `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1`
- No third-party plugins loaded

## Reproducer

`conftest.py`:

```python
import asyncio
import json
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

events = []
allocations = 0


@pytest.fixture
def owner(request):
    global allocations
    allocations += 1
    token = allocations
    events.append(["allocate", request.node.name, token])
    yield token
    events.append(["release", request.node.name, token])


@pytest.fixture
def resource(owner, request):
    yield owner
    if request.node.name == "test_first":
        raise BaseExceptionGroup(
            "cleanup",
            [asyncio.CancelledError("cancel marker"), RuntimeError("ordinary marker")],
        )


def pytest_sessionfinish(session, exitstatus):
    Path("events.json").write_text(json.dumps(events), encoding="utf-8")
```

`test_lifecycle.py`:

```python
def test_first(resource):
    assert resource == 1


def test_next(resource):
    assert resource == 2, "cached function-scoped owner reused"
```

Run from that isolated directory:

```text
PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD=1 python -m pytest test_lifecycle.py -q -p no:cacheprovider
```

On Windows, set `PYTEST_DISABLE_PLUGIN_AUTOLOAD` in the process environment before
running the Python command.

## Actual results and causal comparisons

Each variant runs in a fresh process. Exit code 1 is expected because `test_first`
intentionally has a teardown error; the unexpected effects are the missing owner
finalizers and stale cached value.

| Teardown exception | Owner allocations | Owner releases | Following test |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| `RuntimeError("ordinary marker")` | 2 | 2 | passes with token 2 |
| group of `CancelledError` and `RuntimeError` | 1 | 0 | fails, token 1 reused |
| group of `GeneratorExit` and `RuntimeError` | 1 | 0 | fails, token 1 reused |

For the cancellation variant, `events.json` contains only:

```json
[["allocate", "test_first", 1]]
```

Replacing the cancellation leaf with `GeneratorExit("exit marker")` produces the
same owner-finalization failure. Replacing the whole group with an ordinary
`RuntimeError` produces:

```json
[["allocate", "test_first", 1], ["release", "test_first", 1],
 ["allocate", "test_next", 2], ["release", "test_next", 2]]
```

## Expected

Finish independent fixture owners and invalidate their cached results even when
a finalizer raises one of these groups, then report/propagate the original errors.
The next test should allocate its own function-scoped owner. This request does not
require discarding cancellation/exit leaves or converting them into success.

## Investigation

`FixtureDef.finish` collects `BaseException` and invalidates its own cache.
`SetupState.teardown_exact` catches only `TEST_OUTCOME` while draining the item's
finalizers. A group containing these leaves is outside that catch, so processing
exits after the item has already been removed from the setup stack. Other fixture
finalizers of that item are skipped. The owner fixture retains its cached value.

The current main branch source also retains the narrower catch; this is source
inspection, not a claim that a newer released version has been executed.

No downstream workaround or unverified dependency upgrade has been applied.

issues.title: pytest.approx with a list expected value reports overflowing differences for numpy integer arrays
issues.body:
Comparing a NumPy integer array against `pytest.approx(<python list>)` uses 8-bit arithmetic in the failure report, so the reported differences are wrong and, with `-Werror`, the report degrades to `representation of details failed`. The `approx(<numpy array>)` path unboxes the NumPy scalars (`ApproxNumpy._yield_comparisons` / `_repr_compare`), the sequence path (`ApproxSequenceLike`) does not.

Reproducer (`pytest 10.0.0.dev10+g0212785e3`, numpy 2.3.3):

```python
import numpy as np
import pytest


def test_approx_list_expected_numpy_actual():
    actual = np.array([255], dtype=np.uint8)
    assert actual == pytest.approx([0])
```

`python -m pytest -Werror test_approx_list_expected_numpy_actual.py`:

```
E   RuntimeWarning: overflow encountered in scalar subtract
    result: bool = abs(self.expected - actual) <= self.tolerance
```

Without `-Werror` the test fails, but the message reports the wrong numbers:

```
E       AssertionError:
E       assert array([255], dtype=uint8) == approx([0 ± 1.0e-12])
E         comparison failed. Mismatched elements: 1 / 1:
E         Max absolute difference: 1
E         Max relative difference: 0.00392156862745098
```

The differences come from `ApproxSequenceLike._repr_compare` subtracting a `numpy.uint8` scalar from a Python float, which wraps around (`255 - 0` → `-1`), so the absolute difference is `1` instead of `255`. `int8` is worse: `pytest.approx([127])` against `np.array([-128], dtype=np.int8)` reports `Max relative difference: -0.0078125`.

`pytest.approx(np.array([0], dtype=np.uint8))` against the same array reports `255` and `1.0` correctly, so the two `approx` flavours disagree about the same comparison.

Unboxing the value in the sequence loop as well fixes it:

```python
        for i, (approx_value, other_value) in enumerate(
            zip(approx_side_as_map, other_side, strict=True)
        ):
            other_value = _unbox_numpy_scalar(other_value)
            if approx_value != other_value:
```

It is a no-op for plain Python values, since `_unbox_numpy_scalar` only calls `.item()` when the attribute exists. With that applied both reproducers report `255` / `1.0` and `testing/python/approx.py` still passes.

Related: #15312 fixes the array-expected path only.

issues.title: Improvements to traceback management on custom pytest.Item objects
issues.body:
<!--
Thanks for suggesting a feature!

Quick check-list while suggesting features:
-->

#### What's the problem this feature will solve?
<!-- What are you trying to do, that you are unable to achieve with pytest as it currently stands? -->

I've come across some pain points from working with non python tests by subclassing pytest.Item (as the pytest documentation itself says to do https://docs.pytest.org/en/stable/example/nonpython.html). It's technically three separate things, but they're all interlinked, so I didn't think 3 separate issues were worth it.

Specifically:

* By default, if your test generates an error, it will spit out an extra 500 lines of pytest internals traceback (not even exaggerating, see https://pastebin.com/evrEMka2). This is, as far as I can tell, because the base pytest.Item `_traceback_filter`, inherited from pytest.Node, doesn't do any actual filtering - filter logic is only implemented on `pytest.Function` and `pytest.TestCaseFunction`. It would be nice if the pytest.Node `_traceback_filter`  filtered out pytest internal traceback frames by default (or perhaps pytest.Item can have its own implementation).

* `_traceback_filter` itself is marked as private, or I suppose pseudo-private, as AFAIK python itself does not enforce anything for single underscore prefixed methods, but convention still implies that it's not something library users should be touching. I would like this to be renamed to just `traceback_filter` to make it more clear that it's what the end user is supposed to use to implement filtering, and perhaps it should be mentioned in the documentation.

* If you want to implement your own `_traceback_filter`, and type it correctly, it needs to return the type `Traceback`, but this class is currently not exported via the main module, so you cannot do `from pytest import traceback` but instead must do `from _pytest._code.code import Traceback`, which does work but is certainly ugly, and again, the use of the single underscore implies this isn't something you should be doing.

I am aware you could also implement `repr_failure` on a subclass, but I don't think this should be the only current method for controlling what tracebacks are printed. The current `repr_failure` and `_repr_failure_py` contain a lot of useful boilerplate that special-case certain errors, implement various pytest commandline arguments . . etc. It makes no sense to force the user to either reimplement or give up all this functionality just to be able to filter traceback output. IMO it makes a lot more sense to expect `_traceback_filter` to be implemented as a much neater way to, well, filter tracebacks.

#### Describe the solution you'd like
<!-- A clear and concise description of what you want to happen. -->

As said above
* Provide a default `_traceback_filter` implementation that does not print pytest internals, that almost nobody is realistically going to want, and of course anyone who really does can implement it themselves to control the behaviour.
* Make `_traceback_filter` a public method (ie not starting with "_")
* Make Traceback a public class (ie directly importable from the `pytest` module) (I forgot about this but also TracebackEntry so you can write filter functions)

#### Real world use cases
<!-- Provide examples of real-world use cases that this would enable and how it solves the problem described above. -->

Well I already posted my real world pastebin of how the current status quo spits out 500 lines of junk into the terminal whenever a test fails. These solutions would either A: mean I don't need to write my own `_traceback_filter` by providing a default one, or at least B: mean that when I write one I'm not overriding a seemingly private method (generally considered a no-no) and importing from a seemingly private module (also generally considered a no-no) even if python will not physically stop you from doing either of those.

#### Alternative Solutions
<!-- Have you tried to workaround the problem using a pytest plugin or other tools? Or a different approach to solving this issue? Please elaborate here. -->

As said you could implement your own `repr_failure`, but that comes with drawbacks that I also mentioned. You can also just stick with the status quo and implement your own `_traceback_filter`, python will not _stop_ you, but I do believe that methods that the user would reasonably be expected to want to implement on a subclass should not be marked private.

I did see the issue suggesting adding a hook for traceback filtering (https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest/issues/283), for one it is not yet implemented in pytest, for two I still think that "officially" supporting implementing your own `_traceback_filter` on your own `pytest.Item` subclasses would be helpful.

#### Additional context
<!-- Add any other context, links, etc. about the feature here. -->

issues.title: 9.2.0: INTERNALERROR "'cache/lastfailed' is not allowed to escape the cache directory" when cache_dir contains ".."
issues.body:
### Description

Since 9.2.0, pytest crashes at startup with an `INTERNALERROR` when the cache directory path contains a `..` segment. This happens even though the key being looked up (`cache/lastfailed`) stays inside the cache directory.

A common way to hit this is tox with a `toxworkdir` outside the tox.ini directory (e.g. `toxworkdir=../.tox`). pytest defaults `cache_dir` to `$TOX_ENV_DIR/.pytest_cache`, and tox passes the `..` through verbatim (`/repo/cli/../.tox/py312`). We hit it in https://github.com/aws/aws-parallelcluster/actions/runs/40766983823/job/123093652689?pr=7688, where every pytest job started failing once 9.2.0 was released.

```
INTERNALERROR>   File ".../_pytest/cacheprovider.py", line 334, in __init__
INTERNALERROR>     for k, v in config.cache.get("cache/lastfailed", {}).items()
INTERNALERROR>   File ".../_pytest/cacheprovider.py", line 214, in get
INTERNALERROR>     path = self._getvaluepath(key)
INTERNALERROR>   File ".../_pytest/cacheprovider.py", line 199, in _getvaluepath
INTERNALERROR>     return self._join_within(self._cachedir / self._CACHE_PREFIX_VALUES, key)
INTERNALERROR>   File ".../_pytest/cacheprovider.py", line 175, in _join_within
INTERNALERROR>     raise ValueError(f"{name!r} is not allowed to escape the cache directory")
INTERNALERROR> ValueError: 'cache/lastfailed' is not allowed to escape the cache directory
```

### Minimal reproducer

```
mkdir -p proj/sub && cd proj/sub
echo 'def test_ok(): pass' > test_a.py
printf '[pytest]\ncache_dir = ../.pytest_cache\n' > pytest.ini
pytest -q
```

- pytest 9.1.1: `1 passed`
- pytest 9.2.0: `INTERNALERROR> ValueError: 'cache/lastfailed' is not allowed to escape the cache directory`

You get the same failure without an ini file:

```
TOX_ENV_DIR="$PWD/../.tox/py312" pytest -q
```

### Cause

The containment check added in #14884 (`Cache._join_within`) normalizes the joined path but not `base`:

```python
path = Path(os.path.normpath(base.joinpath(name)))
if not path.is_relative_to(base):
    raise ValueError(...)
```

When `base` is `/proj/sub/../.pytest_cache/v`, `path` becomes `/proj/.pytest_cache/v/cache/lastfailed`. That is no longer lexically relative to the un-normalized `base`, so every key is rejected. `cache_dir_from_config()` / `resolve_from_str()` don't normalize the configured path either.

### Suggested fix

Normalize `base` the same way before the comparison:

```python
base = Path(os.path.normpath(base))
path = Path(os.path.normpath(base.joinpath(name)))
```

Alternatively, normalize `_cachedir` once when the `Cache` is created. With the one-line change applied locally, the reproducer passes and `--lf` works. Escaping keys (`../escape`, `/abs/key`, `a/../../escape`) are still rejected, and a `..` that cancels out (`a/../b`) still works.

### Environment

- pytest 9.2.0 (works on 9.1.1)
- Python 3.10–3.14 on ubuntu-latest (GitHub Actions); reproduced locally with Python 3.12.10 on macOS 26.7.1
- tox 4.67.4 (for the tox variant)

## Description

Since pytest 9.2.0, undoing `monkeypatch.setattr` on an attribute of a `unittest.mock.MagicMock` **deletes** that attribute instead of restoring the original child mock. `MagicMock` remembers deleted attributes, so every later access raises `AttributeError`.

This looks like a side effect of #14969 (fix for #10644): `setattr` now records `oldval` from the target's instance `__dict__`, and `undo()` deletes the attribute when it wasn't there. A `MagicMock` keeps its child mocks in `_mock_children`, not in `__dict__`, so the existing child is recorded as missing and `undo()` calls `delattr()` on it.

It shows up in suites that share module-level mocks (e.g. `sys.modules["pkg"] = MagicMock()` in a `conftest.py`) and patch them with `monkeypatch`. In our suite, one test patching `SomeHelper.get_connection` on a shared mock made ~1,000 later tests error out. It passes on 9.1.1.

issues.title: monkeypatch.setattr on a class's __annotations__ deletes them on undo (Python 3.14)
issues.body:
- [x] a detailed description of the bug or problem you are having
- [x] output of `pip list` from the virtual environment you are using
- [x] pytest and operating system versions
- [x] minimal example if possible

On Python 3.14, undoing `monkeypatch.setattr(SomeClass, "__annotations__", ...)` deletes the class's annotations instead of restoring them. Every later test then sees `SomeClass.__annotations__ == {}`. On 3.13 the same tests pass.

```python
# test_annotations.py
class Config:
    name: str
    size: int


def test_patch_annotations(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr(Config, "__annotations__", {**Config.__annotations__, "extra": bool})
    assert set(Config.__annotations__) == {"name", "size", "extra"}


def test_annotations_restored():
    # Runs after the monkeypatch above has been undone.
    assert Config.__annotations__ == {"name": str, "size": int}
```

```
$ python3.14 -m pytest -q test_annotations.py
.F
    def test_annotations_restored():
>       assert Config.__annotations__ == {"name": str, "size": int}
E       AssertionError: assert {} == {'name': <cla...<class 'int'>}
1 failed, 1 passed
```

**Cause.** For a class target, `MonkeyPatch.setattr` records `target.__dict__.get(name, NOTSET)` as the value to restore. Under PEP 649/749, 3.14 no longer keeps `__annotations__` in the class `__dict__`: it holds `__annotate_func__` and `__annotations_cache__`, and `type.__annotations__` is a data descriptor on the metaclass. So the recorded old value is `NOTSET`, and `undo()` calls `delattr(Config, "__annotations__")`, which on 3.14 clears the annotations for good.

```
>>> class C:
...     a: int
>>> C.__annotations__
{'a': <class 'int'>}
>>> '__annotations__' in C.__dict__, sorted(k for k in C.__dict__ if 'annot' in k)
(False, ['__annotate_func__', '__annotations_cache__'])
```

The same shape affects any attribute served by a data descriptor on the metaclass rather than the class `__dict__`, which #1938 already tracks for `__bases__`. I'm filing this separately because on 3.14 it is now reachable through `__annotations__`, a common thing to patch in tests (TypedDict and dataclass field lists), and the failure is silent: the patched test passes and an unrelated later test fails.

**Status on main.** pytest 9.2.0 and main (a7b2446ee) both fail. #15136 fixes it: with that branch installed, the repro above passes, because a data descriptor on `type(target)` now makes `undo()` write the looked-up value back. So I am not opening a competing PR. If it is useful, I can contribute the 3.14 `__annotations__` case above as a regression test to #15136 (skipped below 3.14), and a changelog line, whichever the maintainers prefer.

The workaround we use meanwhile is `monkeypatch.setitem(Config.__annotations__, "extra", bool)`.

**Environment.** macOS 26.6 (arm64), CPython 3.14.4. `pip list`:

```
iniconfig==2.3.1
packaging==26.3
pluggy==1.7.0
Pygments==2.21.0
pytest==9.2.0
```

_Disclosure: this issue was drafted by Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant, via Claude Code) on behalf of @HipHoff, who approved filing it and takes responsibility for it. The repro was run against pytest 9.2.0, pytest main and the #15136 branch on CPython 3.14.4, and against pytest 9.2.0 on 3.13 (passes)._

issues.body:
- [x] a detailed description of the bug or problem you are having
- [x] output of `pip list` from the virtual environment you are using
- [x] pytest and operating system versions
- [x] minimal example if possible

## Description

With pytest 9.2.0, collecting a module that has `from unittest.mock import call` at module level uses gigabytes of memory and takes tens of seconds if the recursion limit has been raised (some libraries do this at import time, e.g. to 100 000). pytest 9.1.1 collects the same file in well under a second. In a memory-limited CI runner the process is simply killed, with no pytest output.

## Cause

`FixtureManager._find_wrapped_fixture_def` (new in 9.2.0) calls `inspect.unwrap(obj, stop=...)` on every module attribute. It tries to skip mock objects with:

```python
if safe_getattr(obj, "_mock_name", None) is not None:
    return None
```

`unittest.mock.call` is a `_Call` whose `_mock_name` is `None`, and `_Call` returns a new `_Call` for any other attribute, including `__wrapped__`. So the `__wrapped__` chain never ends and `inspect.unwrap` only stops at `sys.getrecursionlimit()` (then raises `ValueError`, which pytest swallows). With the default limit of 1000 this is invisible; with a high limit it allocates one object per step.

```
>>> from unittest.mock import call
>>> call._mock_name is None
True
>>> call.__wrapped__
call.__wrapped__
```

Related, older, closed reports for the same object: #1217, #2188, #2208.

## Minimal example

`conftest.py`:

```python
import sys

sys.setrecursionlimit(100_000)
```

`test_repro.py`:

```python
from unittest.mock import call


def test_trivial():
    assert True
```

```
python -m pytest --collect-only -q -p no:cacheprovider
```

issues.title: `pytest.importorskip(..., defer=True)`: gate on a missing dependency but still collect every test
issues.body:
🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

## Problem

`pytest.importorskip("tables")` at module level stops collection of the whole module, and in a `conftest.py` (#15142, #15143) of the whole directory. The tests behind the gate never show up: no node ids, no parametrization, nothing in `--collect-only` or junit, one skip line per module instead of per test.

Projects that want full collection build it by hand. A scan of 177 popular repos:

| pattern | repos |
|---|---|
| shared `requires_x = pytest.mark.skipif(not has_x, ...)` (e.g. xarray `_importorskip` → `(has_x, requires_x)`, ~1000 uses) | 81 |
| `skipif(not HAS_X)` with a try/except import flag | 57 |
| `pytestmark = pytest.mark.skipif(...)` | 41 |
| custom marker + `pytest_collection_modifyitems` / `pytest_runtest_setup` (gdal `require_driver`, keras, salt) | ~12 |
| per-param gates (pandas `td.skip_if_no`) | 13 |

None of them binds the module for use in fixtures, which is why `x = pytest.importorskip("x")` stays the most common gate: module-level `importorskip` in 939 test modules across 76 repos, and in 10 conftests across 6 repos.

## Hard limit

pytest learns tests by executing the module. A module that uses the dependency at import time (`import X`, `from X import Y`, `@parametrize("f", X.FILTERS)`, `X.__version__` in a decorator) cannot be collected without X, whatever the API. Any solution only helps code that uses the dependency lazily, and must fall back to today's module skip for the rest.

Classifying the 939 gated test modules by what follows the gate:

| after the gate | modules |
|---|---|
| bound name used only inside functions | 339 (36%) |
| bare gate, nothing bound | 238 (25%) |
| bound name used at module scope | 167 (18%) |
| hard `import X` / `from X import Y` | 195 (21%) |

So roughly 40-55% of existing gates would collect fully with no edits (some of the first two groups pull X in transitively through later imports).

## Proposal

Opt-in `defer=True` on `pytest.importorskip`:

```python
tables = pytest.importorskip("tables", defer=True)
```

- **X present:** returns the real module; nothing changes.
- **X missing, called while pytest imports a test module or conftest:** record the gate on that node (the `Module`, or the conftest's directory) and return a stand-in object. Import continues, every test in scope is collected, and each is skipped at setup with the original reason and the gate's location.
- **Fallback:** if the import then fails for any reason (the stand-in used at import time, `from X import Y`, project code importing X), raise the normal module-level skip. That is exactly today's result, because today nothing after the gate runs.
- **Called inside a test or fixture:** unchanged.

Possible companion: a `pytest.mark.requires_import("x", minversion=...)` marker evaluated with the skip marks, replacing the hand-rolled `requires_x` / `skip_if_no` helpers for per-test and per-param cases.

### Implementation sketch

- A context variable for "node currently being imported", set around `importtestmodule` and conftest import; `importorskip(defer=True)` checks it. Without it, `defer=True` behaves like today.
- Gates stored in the node stash; `pytest_runtest_setup` skips an item when any node in `item.listchain()` has a gate.
- The stand-in must raise `AttributeError` for private/dunder names (pytest's own introspection: `__test__`, `pytestmark`, fixture markers) and raise the module skip for any other attribute access during import, so `X.__version__` at module scope degrades to today's behaviour instead of a collection error.
- `-rs` should fold item skips by gate so the summary stays one line per gate.

## Costs

1. Skip counts go from 1 per module to 1 per test (junit, dashboards); `-rs` needs folding.
2. The rest of the module body runs when X is missing (side effects, import time). Import errors after a failed gate are absorbed as today, but side effects are new.
3. The stand-in is not `None` and not a `ModuleType`; `if tables is None` style checks will mislead.
4. Only about half of existing gates benefit without edits; the rest need rewrites (`from X import Y` → `X.Y` in test bodies, module-scope version checks → string `skipif` conditions) or stay module skips.

## Prototype

A ~110-line plugin implementing the above (frame-walking instead of a context variable) collects all tests of lazily-gated modules and of a conftest-gated directory with a fixture using the module, skips each at setup, falls back to module skips for eager use and hard imports, and still reports a real `ImportError` without a gate as a collection error.

Related: #15142, #15143, #4479.

issues.title: tmp_path / tmp_path_factory.mktemp list the whole basetemp on every call: O(N^2) over a session
issues.body:
- [x] a detailed description of the bug or problem you are having - [x] output of `pip list` from the virtual environment you are using - [x] pytest and operating system versions - [x] minimal example if possible `TempPathFactory.mktemp()` (and so `tmp_path`) finds the next free number with `make_numbered_dir()`, which lists the whole base temporary directory on every call. The directory gains entries with every test, so test N lists about 2N entries and a session does O(N^2) work: each test is slower than the one before. #11859 made the listing cheaper but, as it says, "doesn't fix the underlying issue (iterating the directory)". ## Reproducer ```python # test_repro.py: N=1000 pytest -q test_repro.py; then N=2000, N=4000 import os, pytest @pytest.fixture(autouse=True) def workdir(tmp_path_factory): return tmp_path_factory.mktemp("work") @pytest.mark.parametrize("i", range(int(os.environ.get("N", "1000")))) def test_many(i, tmp_path): (tmp_path / "f").write_text("x") ``` ## Numbers Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS (Linux 6.17), ext4, CPython 3.12.3, pytest main (c9bf1edf9), 4 cores, `pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider test_repro.py`, wall-clock seconds, median of 3 runs: | tests | pytest main | with the fix below | same tests without `tmp_path` / `mktemp` | |---|---|---|---| | 1000 | 3.53 | 1.53 | 0.79 | | 2000 | 10.10 | 3.03 | 1.19 | | 4000 | 34.35 | 5.78 | 2.13 | On main, doubling the tests takes 2.9-3.4 times as long. ## Fix sketch (PR to follow) `TempPathFactory` keeps the listing of its own basetemp (names and the directory's `os.stat()`: device, inode, mtime, ctime, link count) and passes it to `make_numbered_dir()` through a private keyword argument. The listing is reused while the stat is unchanged. The factory records its own `mkdir` and the `tmp_path` retention removal in it, keeping the new stat only if the link count changed by exactly one. The numbering rule is unchanged: one more than the highest existing number, with the same case-insensitive matching. The listing is only a hint; `mkdir` decides, and on failure the directory is listed again. Other callers of `make_numbered_dir()`, including the `pytest-of-` session root, are unchanged, and filesystems with 1-2 s timestamps are not cached. The listing lives on the factory, so it is plain per-session state: no lock, no fork handling, and `rm_rf()` does not need to know about it. It could instead live inside `make_numbered_dir()` for every caller, but that makes it global state; I would rather keep it on the factory unless you see it differently. ## Limits - Directory names are unchanged as long as only pytest writes into the basetemp. That covers every ordinary session; each xdist worker has its own basetemp. - If something else (another process, or test code writing into `getbasetemp()` directly) creates or removes entries there within one filesystem clock tick of a `mktemp` call, the root's stat can miss it. A different free number can then be chosen, never an existing directory. The clock tick is about 1-4 ms on Linux before 6.13, and about 16 ms on Windows. On Linux 6.13+ with multigrain timestamps it only happens on tmpfs, for a removal plus a creation within ~1 ms. - In a simulation with a realistic clock (ticks not aligned to milliseconds) and a foreign writer in the same tick, 299 of 1,500 random sequences differed from main at 4 ms, and 1,001 of 1,500 at 16 ms. All names were still unique. With pytest as the only writer, 0 differed. - Tested on Linux only; coarse clocks were simulated. Not tested: Windows, macOS, NFS.

issues.title: Typed FixtureRequest: node type by scope and param type (deferred to an official mypy plugin)
issues.body:
🤖 Written by Claude Opus 5.5 via Claude Code for the pytest maintainers; I prompted it, it did the work, I read it.

Follow-up to #13888 and #15227. `request.node` and `request.param` are typed `Any`. This issue records what can be typed more precisely. **The technical design is deferred until pytest has an official mypy plugin** (related: #9334). Until then, nothing here is planned.

## What the scope guarantees at runtime

From `SubRequest.__init__` / `get_scope_node` / `get_scope_package` in `src/_pytest/fixtures.py`:

| scope | `request.node` | exact? |
|---|---|---|
| function | the `Item` (`Function`, `DoctestItem`, plugin items) | no: `Item`, not `Function` |
| class | `Class`, or the item itself when the test is not in a class | no: `Class \| Item` |
| module | `Module` | yes |
| package | `Package`, or `Session` when there is no package | no: `Package \| Session` |
| session | `Session` | yes |
| callable (dynamic) scope | unknown statically | no |
| test's own `request` | the `Item` | no |

So the scope alone never implies `Function`. The common accesses (`.function`, `.callspec`, `.cls`) would still need narrowing on function-scoped fixtures.

## Without a plugin: generic `FixtureRequest[NodeT, ParamT]`

A prototype made `FixtureRequest` generic over `NodeT` (bound to `Node`) and `ParamT`, both defaulting to `Any`. It uses PEP 696 defaults via `typing_extensions` under `TYPE_CHECKING`, which pytest already does elsewhere. Checked with mypy `--strict` and pyright strict:

- A bare `pytest.FixtureRequest` (all existing code) gives no new errors and no "missing type parameters" error.
- `FixtureRequest[pytest.Function, int]` types `node` as `Function` and `param` as `int`.
- `FixtureRequest[pytest.Session]` flags `request.node.callspec`.
- `mypy src` gives no new errors.

Gaps:
- Subscripting with one argument at runtime (`FixtureRequest[pytest.Function]` without `from __future__ import annotations`) raises `TypeError: Too few arguments` unless the runtime `TypeVar`s have defaults. That needs `typing.TypeVar(default=...)` (3.13+) plus a `__class_getitem__` shim or `typing_extensions` on older versions.
- The annotation is only the user's assertion. A mismatch like `@pytest.fixture(scope="session")` with `request: FixtureRequest[pytest.Function]` is not caught, because type checkers cannot link the decorator's `scope=`/`params=` to the annotation of a named `request` parameter. Overloads can't express it, since `Concatenate` covers only leading positional parameters.

## Needs a plugin

- Inferring `node` from `scope=` and `param` from `params=`, or checking an explicit annotation against them. This needs a mypy plugin hook on the fixture decorator. pyright has no plugin API, so pyright users would only get the explicit generic.
- An option without a plugin that covers both checkers: pytest validates the `request` annotation against scope/params when it registers the fixture, and warns on a mismatch.

The design (generic vs. plugin-only, runtime validation, how to handle dynamic scope) is left for the mypy plugin work.

issues.title: Collecting many file arguments in the same directory re-collects the parent directory once per argument (O(args × siblings); Windows adds a samefile per sibling)
issues.body:
## What's the problem

When many test files from the same directory are passed explicitly on the command line (e.g. a tool that selects "related" tests and runs `pytest a/test_1.py a/test_2.py … a/test_63.py`), collection time grows with *(number of file arguments) × (number of entries in their parent directory)*, even though each file is only collected once.

In `Session.collect` (pytest 9.1.1), each file argument walks its path from the root. For the last level, `handle_dupes` is `False` when the remaining part is a single file path ("files given directly multiple times on the command line should not be deduplicated"), so `_collect_one_node` skips the collection cache for that call. The parent `Dir` is therefore collected again for every file argument: a node is built for every sibling (hook calls such as `pytest_ignore_collect` / `pytest_collect_file` for each entry), and then all but one are pruned.

On Windows the pruning step makes it worse: for every sibling whose path does not match, `samefile_nofollow` is called (the #11895 short-path fallback), i.e. two `lstat` calls per non-matching sibling per argument.

## Measurements (one real-world repo)

Windows 11, Python 3.11.15, pytest 9.1.1, pytest-xdist. Warm tree, single process, `--collect-only`, 122 file arguments of which 63 are in one directory with 141 entries:

| | before | with the workaround below |
|---|---:|---:|
| `perform_collect` total (cProfile) | 22.4 s | 11.8 s |
| `Session.collect` (re-collecting parents + pruning) | 15.2 s | 3.7 s |
| `samefile_nofollow` calls | 44,377 | 9,056 |
| `pytest_collect_file` calls | 17,286 | 4,720 |

Without cProfile, 315 file arguments: 55.7 s → 20.7 s. The collected items (IDs and order) are identical before and after (checked on 9,608 and 38,514 items). Passing a directory instead of files does not trigger this (`Session.collect` ≈ 0.06 s).

## Minimal reproduction (sketch)

```bash
mkdir -p repro/tests && cd repro
for i in $(seq 1 150); do printf 'def test_x():\n    pass\n' > tests/test_$i.py; done
time pytest --collect-only -q tests                       # fast
time pytest --collect-only -q $(ls tests/test_*.py | head -100)   # grows with 100 × 150
```

Measured with exactly this repro on Windows 11 / Python 3.11.15 / pytest 9.1.1 (`-p no:cacheprovider -p no:xdist`, 3 rounds, on a busy machine): directory argument 0.97–1.25 s, 100 file arguments 6.53–7.52 s for 100 trivial tests. (The gap is larger on Windows because of the per-sibling `samefile` fallback.)

## Workaround we use

A `pytest_ignore_collect` hook in `conftest.py` that, when every argument is an existing file path (no `--pyargs`, no plain directory arguments), ignores entries that are neither an argument nor an ancestor of one. Since pytest discards those nodes anyway, the collected items do not change. It cannot reach the rootdir level (no conftest there) or the argument-vs-argument comparisons within the same directory, which is why we think the fix belongs upstream.

## Possible fixes (suggestions)

1. Reuse the collected parent `Dir` result across file arguments (cache the parent level even when the last part is a file), while still not deduplicating the file itself, so the "same file given twice runs twice" behavior is kept.
2. In the pruning loop, compare by name (or `os.path.normcase`) first and only fall back to `samefile` when the names could plausibly refer to the same file (e.g. when an argument looks like a Windows short path).

Related: #11895 (the Windows short-path fallback), #13420 (a different collection slowdown with many paths, fixed by caching `_check_initialpaths_for_relpath`).

issues.title: Subtest durations become negative when `time` is mocked (subtests.py bypasses `_pytest.timing`)
issues.body:
- [x] a detailed description of the bug or problem you are having
- [x] output of `pip list` from the virtual environment you are using
- [x] pytest and operating system versions
- [x] minimal example if possible

## Description

When a test mocks `time.perf_counter` / `time.time` (as clock-mocking libraries like freezegun and time-machine do), subtests report negative durations and a stop timestamp of `0.0` (January 1, 1970). Normal tests are unaffected by the same mocking.

## Reproducer

```python
# test_repro.py
import time

def test_normal(monkeypatch):
    real_sleep = time.sleep
    monkeypatch.setattr(time, "perf_counter", lambda: 0.0)
    monkeypatch.setattr(time, "time", lambda: 0.0)
    real_sleep(0.3)

def test_with_subtest(subtests, monkeypatch):
    real_sleep = time.sleep
    with subtests.test(msg="frozen clock"):
        monkeypatch.setattr(time, "perf_counter", lambda: 0.0)
        monkeypatch.setattr(time, "time", lambda: 0.0)
        real_sleep(0.3)
```

```
$ pytest -q --junitxml=out.xml
.u.                                                                      [100%]
2 passed, 1 subtests passed in 1.23s

$ grep -o 'name="[^"]*" time="[^"]*"' out.xml
name="test_normal" time="0.301"
name="test_with_subtest" time="-1194.217"
```

Both tests sleep 0.3s under a mocked clock. The normal test reports 0.301s; the subtest reports −1194s (the exact value depends on the machine's uptime).

## Cause

Normal test execution and subtests handle timing differently.

In `src/_pytest/runner.py`, pytest uses `timing.Instant()` and `instant.elapsed()` from `_pytest.timing`. However, `src/_pytest/subtests.py` imports the `time` module directly and calls `time.time()` and `time.perf_counter()`:

```
$ grep -n "time\." src/_pytest/subtests.py
219:        self._start = time.time()
220:        self._precise_start = time.perf_counter()
245:        precise_stop = time.perf_counter()
247:        stop = time.time()
```

`_pytest.timing` imports `perf_counter` directly using `from time import perf_counter`, so it keeps its original function reference even if `time.perf_counter` is patched later. `subtests.py` looks up the function on the `time` module whenever it is called, so it picks up the patched value.

So if a subtest starts on the real clock and the test then patches `time.perf_counter` to return `0.0`, the subtest computes its duration from the real start time and the patched end time, giving a negative duration. The same happens with `time.time()`, giving a stop timestamp of `0.0`.

This is the situation `_pytest.timing` exists to prevent. Its docstring says pytest grabs time functions internally "to avoid tests mocking "time" to affect pytest runtime information (issue #185)", and #7764 covered the freezegun case for `--durations`. The subtests module, merged later, doesn't follow that rule.

## Proposed fix

Switch `subtests.py` to `timing.Instant()` / `.elapsed()`, matching `runner.py`. If this approach sounds right, I'd be happy to send a PR with a regression test.

## Related

#14412 (fixed in #14670) addressed how subtest timings are aggregated in the terminal with `console_output_style='times'`. This is a separate problem: the timing values themselves are wrong when `time` is mocked, and it still reproduces on main after #14670.

## Environment

- pytest `9.2.0.dev388+g420cf37a3` (main, editable install)
- Python 3.10.12
- Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS
